compatibility.intro: The N62B44 was BMW's mainstream 4.4‑litre V8 throughout the 2000s, fitted across the 5 Series, 6 Series, 7 Series and X5 range. It was BMW's first V8 with continuously variable VANOS on both intake and exhaust camshafts.

failures.title: BMW N62B44 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Valve stem seal failure - oil consumption
items.whatHappens: The N62 is notorious for valve stem seal wear, leading to excessive oil consumption and blue smoke on startup. This is the single most common issue across the N62 family and is caused by the valve stem seals hardening and losing their sealing ability. Symptoms include oil consumption of 1 litre per 1,000 miles or more, blue smoke when starting from cold, and fouled spark plugs.
items.repairVsReplace: Valve stem seal replacement is a substantial job (around £1,500-£3,000) but far cheaper than a full engine replacement. Many owners also address the coolant system and alternator bracket gasket while the intake manifold is off. → Read our full valve stem seal failure guide

items.title: Alternator bracket gasket leak
items.whatHappens: The alternator bracket gasket is a known failure point on the N62. When it fails, oil leaks from the bracket and can drip onto the exhaust, causing a burning smell. In severe cases, it can lead to oil pressure issues.
items.repairVsReplace: The gasket is replaceable (around £300-£600 at an independent specialist) - it's a labour‑intensive job but not engine‑replacing.

items.title: Cooling system leaks
items.whatHappens: The N62's cooling system is under significant stress, with coolant leaks from the expansion tank, radiator, water pump and coolant pipes being common. The V8 layout and tight engine bay make access challenging.
items.repairVsReplace: Individual components are replaceable; a full cooling system overhaul (water pump, thermostat, expansion tank, hoses) is often the most cost‑effective approach at higher mileages.

variants.title: N62B44 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: The N62 family consists of several displacement variants. Within the N62B44, there are two main sub‑variants distinguished by power output and model application. INTRO: The N62B44 covers several closely related 4.4‑litre V8 variants. The critical difference is the power output and which model family the engine was fitted to. - Fitted to: E65 745i / 745Li, E53 X5 4.4i (pre‑facelift), E60 545i - Key technical difference: 333 hp (245 kW) @ 6,100 rpm; 450 Nm torque. This is the original N62B44 specification, with standard VANOS and a 10.5:1 compression ratio. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above - valve stem seals, alternator bracket gasket, cooling system. The 333 hp variant is the most common N62B44 in the UK. - Interchange note: The N62B44A is interchangeable with N62B44B with appropriate ECU and engine management adjustments. - Fitted to: E63/E64 645Ci, E60 545i (late), some post‑facelift E53 X5 4.4i - Key technical difference: 342 hp (252 kW) @ 6,100 rpm; 450 Nm torque. The power increase comes from revised engine mapping, improved intake and exhaust flow, and slightly higher compression in some versions. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above. Later production (2007‑2010) may have improved valve stem seal materials, but the failure remains common. - Interchange note: The N62B44B is a direct swap for N62B44A with ECU programming. Also shares ancillaries with the N62B48 (4.8‑litre) in some applications. RELATED FAMILY MEMBERS: - N62B40 - 4.0‑litre variant, fitted to E65 735i and E53 X5 4.0i - N62B48 - 4.8‑litre variant, fitted to E70 X5 4.8i, E63 650i and E66 750i Similar‑looking codes it is commonly confused with: - BMW N62B48 - the 4.8‑litre version, fitted to 650i and 750i models; similar architecture but larger displacement and higher power - BMW N62B40 - the 4.0‑litre version, fitted to E65 735i; not a direct swap - BMW N63B44 - the turbocharged successor; completely different hot‑vee architecture

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement N62B44 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used N62B44 makes sense only with documented service history using BMW LL‑01 5W‑30 or 5W‑40 oil, evidence of valve stem seal replacement if over 80,000 miles, and a coolant system that has been maintained. The primary risk with used units is undisclosed valve stem seal wear (oil consumption) - insist on a cold start smoke test and compression check before purchase. For lower‑value E53 X5 or E65 7 Series examples (sub‑£3,000), a used engine with documented history can be a cost‑effective option. View used engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper N62B44 recon includes new valve stem seals, alternator bracket gasket, full cooling system overhaul (water pump, thermostat, expansion tank, hoses), VANOS seals and all gaskets. This is the right call for most replacements - you get a like‑new unit with the known weak points already addressed, backed by 12-24 months warranty. View reconditioned engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high‑value, collectable or low‑mileage E63 6 Series, E60 M5 (N62‑related) or limited‑production models where originality matters. For standard applications, reconditioned is usually more cost‑effective. View rebuilt engines

items.question: Is the N62B44 more reliable than the N63B44?
items.answer: The N62B44 is generally considered more reliable than the later N63B44 hot-vee turbo V8. The N62's naturally aspirated design is simpler and more accessible for repairs, while the N63's hot-vee layout generates significant heat that can cause valve stem seal, turbo coolant line and battery drain issues. However, the N62 has its own well-documented valve stem seal and cooling system problems. → Compare N62B44 vs N63B44 reliability

N63 offers more power but more complexity
Both require careful maintenance for longevity
